Definition — Linear, sublinear and quadratic convergence
      
        Errors $e_k\to0$ converge linearly (geometrically) with rate $q\in(0,1)$ if $e_{k+1}\le q\,e_k$, so $e_k\le q^ke_0$; sublinearly if slower than every geometric rate, typically $e_k\le C/k^p$; quadratically if $e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^2$ (Newton's method near a solution).

entire_proposed.source_text:
Definition — Linear, sublinear and quadratic convergence
      
        Nonnegative errors $e_k\to0$ converge linearly (geometrically) with rate $q\in(0,1)$ if $e_{k+1}\le q\,e_k$, so $e_k\le q^ke_0$; sublinearly if slower than every geometric rate, for example $e_k=C/k^p$ with $C,p\gt0$ and $k\ge1$ (a polynomial upper bound alone does not rule out geometric convergence); quadratically if $e_{k+1}\le Ce_k^2$ with $C\gt0$ (scalar Newton's method near a regular root of a $C^2$ function, from a sufficiently close initial point).

entire_current.source_text: Reaching $e_k\le\varepsilon$ takes $k\ge\ln(e_0/\varepsilon)/\ln(1/q)$ iterations at a linear rate, growing like $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, but $k\ge1/\varepsilon^2$ for $1/\sqrt k$. For $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$, $e_0=1$: $20$ iterations at $q=0.5$ against $10^{12}$. On a logarithmic plot a linear rate is a straight line, a sublinear one flattens (see the explorer). Used for geometric Lyapunov decay and interior-point iteration counts $O(\sqrt n\log(1/\varepsilon))$ in Module 2, $O(1/\sqrt T)$ primal-dual rates in Module 8, and gradient descent in Primer B.

entire_proposed.source_text: For $e_0,\varepsilon\gt0$, the geometric envelope $q^ke_0$ is at most $\varepsilon$ iff $k\ge\ln(e_0/\varepsilon)/\ln(1/q)$; this cutoff suffices for any errors $e_k\le q^ke_0$, and grows like $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ with fixed $q\in(0,1)$ and $e_0$. For the exact errors $e_k=1/\sqrt k$, $k\ge1$, reaching the tolerance is equivalent to $k\ge1/\varepsilon^2$. At $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$ and $e_0=1$, the two exact envelopes first reach the tolerance at $20$ iterations for $q=0.5$ and at $10^{12}$, respectively; faster errors can reach it earlier. On a logarithmic plot exact positive geometric errors form a straight line, while the logarithmic slope of a positive reciprocal-power curve tends to zero (see the explorer). Used for geometric Lyapunov decay and interior-point iteration counts $O(\sqrt n\log(1/\varepsilon))$ in Module 2, $O(1/\sqrt T)$ primal-dual rates in Module 8, and gradient descent in Primer B.
